articles.title: FUJIFILM’s Spectrum tour enthrals visual creators, photography enthusiasts in Bengaluru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The three-day event featured specialised experience zones focusing on distinct creative mediums, including vlogging, cinematography, street photography and portraiture
A multi-city FUJIFILM India Spectrum Tour, bringing together of the brand’s entire range of imaging solutions from Instax cameras, digital cameras and lenses, concluded in Bengaluru recently.

The three-day event, held at the Venkatappa Art Gallery, featured specialised experience zones focusing on distinct creative mediums, including vlogging, cinematography, street photography and portraiture, attracted a large number of people.

Company executives highlighted the regional strategy behind selecting the city for this segment of the tour. "We are excited to connect with the city’s vibrant imaging community. Through Spectrum, we aim to bring our imaging heritage and cutting-edge technology closer to creators,"’ said Koji Wada, managing director of FUJIFILM India.

The tour was in Bengaluru after Gurugram and Ahmedabad, attracting local photography enthusiasts, visual creators and students who prefer to have a hands-on experience with FUJIFILM product ranges. A central component involved educational masterclasses led by established industry practitioners. Photographers including Sudhir Ramachandran and Prashant Godbole were among the participants.

Sessions covered architectural, landscape, and street photography. Other sessions led by technical experts covered niche genres such as astrophotography, wildlife documentation, and sports imaging. The event consolidated the company’s various product categories, including mirrorless camera systems, instant photography devices, and optical tools, under a unified interactive environment.

Arun Babu, associate director of the Imaging Solutions Division at FUJIFILM India, said, “In Bengaluru, through hands-on experiences, we encouraged visitors to experiment with our imaging solutions and discover new ways to express their creativity.”

articles.title: Kashmir’s famed saffron fields have been used as dumping grounds for three years: Mehbooba Mufti
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister says nearly 2,000 kanals of land have been damaged, threatening the livelihoods of 150 families; the NGT has directed a panel to inspect the site and recommend action

The committee will examine the extent of pollution caused by the waste dumping, assess its impact on saffron cultivation spread over approximately 2,000 kanals of land and adjoining areas, and ascertain whether the dumping site has obtained the requisite statutory clearances, officials said

articles.title: Immigration officers make arrest at Seattle airport in ‘distressing’ scene, delaying flight
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred"

Masked immigration officers detained at least one person on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday (November 22, 2026) as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognise how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."
It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect".
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities".

articles.title: South Korea Education Minister resigns amid AI cheating scandal
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday (November 15, 2026), when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score
South Korea's Education Minister resigned on Sunday (November 22, 2026) over an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted ahead of the country's key college entrance exams last week.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday (November 15, 2026), when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial college entrance exam known as the Suneung.
The annual nine-hour Suneung is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.

The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures — including blocking public Wi-Fi in testing areas and placing stickers over clothing buttons but Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin struggled to reassure the public, particularly after remarks he made three days before the exam.

"The exam concluded without any major incidents... However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance," Mr. Choi wrote on X.
"Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation," he added.
President Lee Jae Myung has accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday (November 16, 2026) whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old replied: "Due to my age, I am not confident I could."
Mr. Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday's (November 19, 2026) exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday's (November 19, 2026) exam, nearly half of which were detected through three emergency alerts sent by the government to identify smartphones that test takers had failed to hand over.

articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Leaders of the U.S., Russia and China agreed to begin talks on nuclear risk reduction but offered no details on institutionalising the dialogue process

While addressing the press after the November 19 summit with American and Chinese leaders in Shenzhen, the Chinese tech hub, Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to comparisons between the trilateral and the 1945 Yalta Conference . “What was wrong with Yalta? What was so bad about it?” he said, while responding to a question. “At Yalta, the victory over Nazism was codified... I wouldn’t mind — in fact, I would consider it right — to codify a victory over ‘neo-Nazism’ as well,” Mr. Putin said.

At the Yalta Conference, one of the most consequential diplomatic summits of the 20th century, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, American President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill assembled in the Crimean city to discuss the post-war political order. In February 1945, when the summit was held, the Soviet Red Army had pushed deep into Eastern Europe and was marching towards Berlin while the Allied forces were advancing from Western Europe. The defeat of Nazi Germany was certain. The leaders decided that Germany would be divided, German militarism would be eliminated, and Nazi institutions would be dismantled. The summit played an important role in shaping the post-war European order.

In 1799, the British physician Francis Buchanan recorded that Muslims “long settled in Arakan” called themselves the “Rooinga”.

Many joined them, coming from Chittagong during colonial rule. articles.title: News in Frames | Living with the wounds of displacement

fullParagraphs: The ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is significant, but refugees continue to face the threat of violence and restrictions on humanitarian access, as the situation in their homeland remains precarious

T he International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN’s top court, on November 19, ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during the military’s 2017 clearance operations in Rakhine State. This was the first time the world court held a country responsible for committing genocide.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority, have faced decades of systematic discrimination in the Southeast Asian country, including the denial of citizenship, restrictions on movement and access to education, healthcare and livelihoods.

In August 2017, a military crackdown involving mass killings, sexual violence, and the burning of villages forced more than 7,40,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. They joined earlier waves of refugees who had escaped persecution. Nearly 1.2 million Rohingya now live in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar. Rohingya refugees in other countries such as India, Malaysia and Indonesia also face uncertain legal status, discrimination, detention and the threat of deportation.
Meanwhile, their homeland remains deeply troubled. Rakhine State has been engulfed in fighting between Myanmar’s military and the Arakan Army, a rebel group which now controls much of the region.

The Rohingya, many of whom remain internally displaced, face renewed insecurity, restrictions on humanitarian access and the threat of violence from competing armed forces. And for the refugees, a return to their homeland is neither desirable nor practical. While the ICJ verdict is significant and sets a strong precedent, it is unlikely to ease the suffering of the Rohingya.

Seeking safe harbour: The refugees being transported by a wooden boat to a temporary shelter in Krueng Raya, Aceh Besar, Indonesia, on April 8, 2013. The port has been a major landing point and temporary shelter site over the years.
Fleeing the inferno: Rohingya refugees flee as fires in Myanmar, allegedly started by the military, burn in the background, near Bangladesh in 2017.
Paddling into exile: Rohingya refugees cross the Naf River on an improvised raft to reach Bangladesh on November 12, 2017.
Longing for justice: Rohingya refugees watch the live announcement of the verdict in a genocide case against Myanmar on November 19, 2026
The agony of loss: Hamida, a Rohingya refugee, weeps as she holds her 40-day-old son, who died after their boat capsized before reaching the shore in Teknaf, Bangladesh, on September 14, 2017.

articles.title: How U.S. controls flow of advanced tech, chip, and compute to China | Explained
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The U.S. Commerce Department on November 16 issued an interim final rule barring data centre operators outside the U.S. equipped with advanced American AI chips from providing cloud service to businesses in two dozen countries, including China, Iran, and Russia

The story so far: The battle for the most-sought-after commodity that underpins development of artificial intelligence technology just grew fiercer. On November 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim final rule (IFR) requiring companies to have licences to supply advanced American AI chips to data centre operators outside the U.S. with substantial computing power to businesses headquartered in two dozen countries, including China, Iran, and Russia. The new rule restricts American companies from freely shipping high-end AI chips to a set of five countries, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore, without the explicit approval of the U.S. government.

China has censured the move, calling it “yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry”. The interim rule came just days ahead of the meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit.

The U.S. government’s policy on making advanced technology inaccessible to China has been a talking point among lawmakers in Washington for well over a decade, but Congress strengthened the extant legal framework only during the first Trump term when it passed the Export Control Reform Act in 2018.

It strengthened the U.S. government’s authority to control the movement of advanced technology originating in the country, and included curbing exports of sensitive technologies, including top-tier chips, with dual-use — both commercial and military — applications to countries such as China, Russia, and Iran.

A year later, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Chinese telecom equipment maker Huawei and its affiliates on the Entity List, effectively blocking their access to high-end semiconductors.

articles.title: Medicos warn against craze for fairness after 17-year-old Keralam girl diagnosed with kidney disorder
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early
The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.

A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.

The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.

Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.

Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.

“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.

A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.

Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.

articles.title: Specialised training on the anvil for college teachers, staff in Calicut varsity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Proposals form part of the ASCENT project planned to mark the institution’s diamond jubilee; the university’s Syndicate is expected to consider them soon

The University of Calicut is planning to organise specialised training programmes for teachers and staff in its affiliated colleges at foundational and advanced levels. A curriculum that incorporates interdisciplinary approaches is in the pipeline too.

According to university sources, this is part of the ASCENT (Advancing Standards for College Empowerment and Transformation) project being planned to mark the diamond jubilee of the institution. The university’s Syndicate is expected to consider the proposals soon.

The sources say that the training will be provided in areas such as enhancing the operational excellence of colleges, digital office management, securing research grants, and improving the rankings by the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) and the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF).

A university official says that a special mechanism has been proposed to prepare colleges that have not yet received NAAC or NIRF accreditation or rankings. A transparent digital rating system based on NAAC and NIRF criteria is likely to be introduced to enable the assessment of the academic standards of colleges and the monitoring of their progress.

There is plan to introduce certificate and diploma courses in collaboration with recognised industrial establishments alongside regular degree programmes. The objective is to ensure that the students acquire additional skills and become job-ready in fields such as Artificial Intelligence, fintech, and digital media.

The project also includes an institutional enterprise resource planning system being developed by the Calicut University Computer Centre. This software, which digitises academic and administrative processes ranging from admissions to the recording of marks, will be made available to colleges at an affordable rate.

A premium tri-monthly publication is also proposed to be launched under the public relations wing to introduce the achievements of the university and its affiliated colleges at the national and international levels. The sources say that the ASCENT project is envisioned to make the colleges active participants in the development process. The proposal were prepared by a team led by the Vice-Chancellor, pro-Vice-Chancellor, and the Director of the College Development Council.

articles.title: Federation of Islamic Organisations and Political Parties welcomes T.N. govt.’s review petition in Thirupparankundram case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Federation of Islamic Organisations and Political Parties on Sunday welcomed the Tamil Nadu government’s decision to file a review petition in the Supreme Court against its interim order on November 20 that allowed lighting of the lamp at the deepathoon on Karthigai Deepam day as an one time arrangement.

The Federation held a meeting in Chennai on Sunday to discuss further course of action in the Thirupparankundram issue. Sources said during the meeting, the Federation urged the Tamil Nadu government to ensure that usual practice of lighting the lamp should be followed this year too, and that permission should be granted only to light it at the customary spot near the Uchchi Pillaiyar temple.

The Federation also said the Tamil Nadu government has a responsibility to protect communal harmony in the Thirupparankundram issue. It urged the government to engage senior advocates to argue the case and ensure the long-standing practice of lighting the lamp was continued.

Political & National Report: Federation of Islamic Organisations and Political Parties welcomes T.N. govt.’s review petition in Thirupparankundram case. This development is a key milestone in India's ongoing legislative, judicial, and constitutional governance framework.

articles.title: AI centre to come up in Vijayapura
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: MLC and general secretary of the BLDE Association Sunilgouda Patil and co-founder of Sarvam AI Vivek Raghavan exchange MoU documents
BLDE Association (BLDEA) plans to set up an Artificial Intelligence (AI) centre of excellence in Vijayapura to boost AI-based education, technology and innovation in North Karnataka.
BLDEA signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI for the purpose in Bengaluru recently.
The centre will come up at the BLDE Association Vachanapitamaha Dr. P.G. Halakatti College of Engineering and Technology (BLDEACET).
MLC and general secretary of BLDE Association Sunilgouda Patil and co-founder of Sarvam AI Vivek Raghavan exchanged the documents at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.

“The establishment of this center aims to provide training in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning and Generative AI and start-up incubation to students and faculty from the various educational institutions of BLDEA and to students from Vijayapura and other parts of North Karnataka,” Mr. Patil said.

“In collaboration with experts from Sarvam AI, the center will offer industry-oriented training, experiential learning, project-based work, internships and certification courses. Furthermore, it will encourage the development of AI-based products and solutions by providing mentorship and necessary support to student start-ups, young entrepreneurs and innovators. A key objective of this center is to bridge the technology and skills gap between Bengaluru and Tier-II cities, thereby creating new employment and entrepreneurial opportunities for talented youth right here in North Karnataka,” he said.

IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge, who was present, expressed his appreciation, noting that such centers will help the youth of North Karnataka take the lead in the new era of Artificial Intelligence and demonstrate their potential within the technology sector.
Principal of the college P. Manjunath, Chairperson of the AI ​​Centre of Excellence R.P.B. Kotnal and others were present.

articles.title: Migratory birds flock to Kawal Tiger Reserve as winter sets in
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Recent sightings of five migratory species highlight the ecological importance of the reserve’s forests, grasslands and wetlands

The arrival of migratory birds from Siberia, Central Asia and other northern regions has brought renewed attention to the ecological significance of Kawal Tiger Reserve (KTR) in the erstwhile combined Adilabad district, with five species recorded in the Jannaram Forest Division and adjoining areas over the past few days.

The Siberian Stonechat, Red-headed Bunting, Olive-backed Pipit, Garganey and Northern Pintail were among the winter visitors documented jointly by Jannaram Forest Divisional Officer (FDO) M. Ram Mohan and wildlife researcher and Hyderabad Tiger Conservation Society (HyTiCoS) coordinator Venkat Anagandhula.
The sightings, recorded both within and outside the reserve’s forest areas, highlight the importance of Kawal’s diverse habitats in supporting migratory birds.

Among the recent arrivals, the Red-headed Bunting (Emberiza bruniceps), a small migratory bird distinguished by its reddish-brown head and yellow body, breeds in Central Asia before migrating to the Indian subcontinent during winter. It generally inhabits open scrublands, grasslands and agricultural fields, feeding on seeds, grains and insects.

The Olive-backed Pipit (Anthus hodgsoni), which breeds in the Himalayan region and parts of northern and eastern Asia, migrates southwards during winter. It prefers woodland edges, forest clearings and scrub habitats, where it feeds on insects, small invertebrates and seeds.

The Siberian Stonechat (Saxicola maurus), another winter visitor to Telangana, travels from its breeding grounds in Siberia and Central and northern Asia. The species is commonly found in grasslands, scrublands, agricultural fields and wetland edges, feeding primarily on insects.

The Garganey (Spatula querquedula) and Northern Pintail (Anas acuta), both migratory dabbling ducks, have also been recorded in the Kawal landscape. These species breed in northern regions and migrate to the Indian subcontinent during winter, seeking freshwater wetlands, reservoirs and shallow water bodies that provide suitable feeding grounds.

The Annual Waterbird Census conducted between January 3 and 18, 2026, which covered selected freshwater ecosystems within and around Kawal Tiger Reserve in the erstwhile Adilabad district, documented more than 70 species of waterbirds, including resident birds, winter visitors and passage migrants.
The census recorded species such as the Northern Pintail, Common Redshank, Red-crested Pochard, Common Teal, Cotton Pygmy Goose, sandpipers and Temminck’s Stint.

Recent sightings of five migratory species highlight the ecological importance of the reserve’s forests, grasslands and wetlands

The arrival of migratory birds from Siberia, Central Asia and other northern regions has brought renewed attention to the ecological significance of Kawal Tiger Reserve (KTR) in the erstwhile combined Adilabad district, with five species recorded in the Jannaram Forest Division and adjoining areas over the past few days.

The Siberian Stonechat, Red-headed Bunting, Olive-backed Pipit, Garganey and Northern Pintail were among the winter visitors documented jointly by Jannaram Forest Divisional Officer (FDO) M. Ram Mohan and wildlife researcher and Hyderabad Tiger Conservation Society (HyTiCoS) coordinator Venkat Anagandhula.

The sightings, recorded both within and outside the reserve’s forest areas, highlight the importance of Kawal’s diverse habitats in supporting migratory birds.

Among the recent arrivals, the Red-headed Bunting (Emberiza bruniceps), a small migratory bird distinguished by its reddish-brown head and yellow body, breeds in Central Asia before migrating to the Indian subcontinent during winter. It generally inhabits open scrublands, grasslands and agricultural fields, feeding on seeds, grains and insects.

The Olive-backed Pipit (Anthus hodgsoni), which breeds in the Himalayan region and parts of northern and eastern Asia, migrates southwards during winter. It prefers woodland edges, forest clearings and scrub habitats, where it feeds on insects, small invertebrates and seeds.

The Siberian Stonechat (Saxicola maurus), another winter visitor to Telangana, travels from its breeding grounds in Siberia and Central and northern Asia. The species is commonly found in grasslands, scrublands, agricultural fields and wetland edges, feeding primarily on insects.

The Garganey (Spatula querquedula) and Northern Pintail (Anas acuta), both migratory dabbling ducks, have also been recorded in the Kawal landscape. These species breed in northern regions and migrate to the Indian subcontinent during winter, seeking freshwater wetlands, reservoirs and shallow water bodies that provide suitable feeding grounds.

The Annual Waterbird Census conducted between January 3 and 18, 2026, which covered selected freshwater ecosystems within and around Kawal Tiger Reserve in the erstwhile Adilabad district, documented more than 70 species of waterbirds, including resident birds, winter visitors and passage migrants.

The census recorded species such as the Northern Pintail, Common Redshank, Red-crested Pochard, Common Teal, Cotton Pygmy Goose, sandpipers and Temminck’s Stint.

Some migratory birds travel thousands of kilometres to reach their wintering grounds in India, where they generally remain until March before returning to their breeding habitats.

articles.title: Myanmar calls ASEAN review of peace plan 'unfair and imbalanced'; questions bloc's treatment
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Myanmar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the review and recommendations adopted at the ASEAN Summit in Manila did not reflect the positive measures undertaken by the country

Myanmar has termed the ASEAN leaders' assessment of its implementation of a five-point peace plan "unfair and imbalanced", accusing the regional bloc of disregarding its views and denying it equal rights and representation as a member state.

In a statement issued on Saturday (November 21, 2026), Myanmar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the review and recommendations adopted at the ASEAN Summit in Manila on November 15, 2026 did not adequately reflect the positive measures undertaken by the country.

"Although ASEAN has yet to reach a consensus, Myanmar continues to engage bilaterally with individual ASEAN Member states," the Ministry said, expressing appreciation to members that had extended support and assistance in recognition of what it described as positive developments in the country.

The statement comes after ASEAN leaders reiterated their concern over insufficient progress in implementing the five-point peace plan agreed upon in April 2021 following the military takeover in Myanmar.
They also extended restrictions on the country's leadership attending the bloc's summits, saying the ban would remain until there was meaningful progress in implementing the plan.
Under the arrangement, Myanmar can be represented at ASEAN summits only by a non-political representative, such as a career diplomat.

The five-point consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among all parties, an ASEAN special envoy to facilitate mediation, a visit by the envoy to Myanmar to meet all parties, and humanitarian assistance through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management.

The conflict in Myanmar has continued since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, triggering widespread protests, a military crackdown and an armed resistance movement.

ASEAN's five-point consensus was adopted in April 2021 in an attempt to end the violence and facilitate a peaceful resolution to the crisis. However, the bloc has repeatedly expressed frustration over the lack of progress in its implementation.
Rejecting criticism of its handling of the conflict, Myanmar said it had continued to cooperate with ASEAN's suggestions and recommendations while safeguarding its national interests and sovereignty.

articles.title: U.S. deportees in South Sudan went hungry as guards pocketed money from relatives, families say
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees' families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones

Migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries other than their own have endured hunger, thirst and other deprivations while being detained indefinitely in places with poor human rights records and little oversight.
For those expelled to South Sudan, and their families, the ordeal has come at an additional cost.

Guards have solicited and received thousands of dollars from detainees' families, who were told the money would be used to improve conditions for their loved ones. Instead, the guards pocketed most of the money, families said, while detainees went for days without food or clean water, and months held incommunicado.

“They used our desperate situation,” said Ngoc Phan, a U.S. citizen whose husband Tuan Phan had been detained in South Sudan for nearly a year before he was repatriated to Vietnam in June. “If that's not exploitation, I don't know what is.”
It is the inevitable outcome, she said, of a U.S. immigration policy that places deportees in the custody of countries struggling with poverty and corruption, then looks the other way.

Five deportees remain in custody in South Sudan, a country in East Africa where millions face severe hunger and poverty after years of civil conflict and devastating floods. The economy is in tatters, and government workers rarely receive wages.

In all, Ms. Ngoc Phan said she forked over roughly $4,000 intended for food, water and a cellphone. She sent several hundred dollars on multiple occasions and each time, her husband said, guards would give him a few bananas and apples, and some peanuts.

Mr. Tuan Phan, 44, said he lost 20 pounds while under confinement at a gated three-story building in Juba, the capital, and that tensions grew between detainees and guards as living conditions worsened.

One detainee who wanted a window open for fresh air was struck in the face by a guard, and another who complained about a lack of soap was locked in his room for days and only let out to eat, he said.

In addition to the Phans, The Associated Press interviewed six other people familiar with the treatment of detainees in South Sudan, including relatives and lawyers. Most spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation against the detainees.

articles.title: EU will ‘not endorse’ climate deal, throwing COP31 outcome into doubt
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Ireland’s Climate and Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien said the EU would not back an Antalya Pact that “does not even mention fossil fuels”, as the UN climate talks ran into record extra time
The European Union on Sunday (November 22, 2026) rejected a climate deal that omits any mention of fossil fuels , as the UN climate talks in Türkiye pushed into record extra time.
Ireland’s Climate and Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said the EU and its member States “object” to the pact because it “does not meet the moment”.

“We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” Mr. O’Brien told a chaotic closing session a record 44 hours after the summit’s official end. Panama, a vocal critic of the COP process that had threatened to walk away from the talks, also formally objected to the proposed deal as the summit plunged into a tumultuous finale.

The proposed deal needs consensus approval from nearly 200 nations, but many States had expressed frustration that the draft did not refer to coal, oil or gas. “We will not accept negotiating backwards in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” said Mr. O’Brien.

Ahead of the closing session, COP31 President and Türkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum had urged parties to find a compromise, after nearly two weeks of grinding negotiations led to a complete stalemate in the final moments.

“We had negotiations and we listened to everyone patiently,” Mr. Kurum told the final plenary. “We wanted to give a good message to the rest of the world.” Fossil fuels are a flashpoint at the climate talks, which come against a difficult backdrop of soaring energy prices and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran.

With expectations low, negotiations chief Australia had sought an overarching political agreement to capture what countries agreed at COP31 and send a signal about the future course of climate action. But the EU and island nations threatened by rising seas protested after a proposed text did not mention fossil fuels by name.
Language around fossil fuels is fiercely opposed by petro-States such as oil-rich Saudi Arabia. A Saudi official declined to comment when approached by AFP .

Threats of a walkout on Saturday (November 21, 2026) prompted Türkiye and Australia to convene a hurried meeting between the EU and Saudi Arabia, but a compromise remained elusive. The latest text introduces an oblique reference to a previous global deal in 2023 to shift the world away from fossil fuels, but stops short of naming them explicitly.

The text also proposed retaining a contentious push to expand carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised as costly and ineffective in cutting emissions. Climate campaigners had urged countries to reject the deal. “This text isn’t a climate plan. It’s a licence to keep polluting,” said Sara Shaw of the environmental group 350.org.

articles.title: Rebels kill 15 in South Sudan
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: An official hinted at fighters loyal to the country's former first Vice-President Riek Machar, a longtime rival of President Salva Kiir who has been under house arrest since March 2025
An attack on Sunday (November 22, 2026) by rebels in northwestern South Sudan has killed at least 15 civilians, with the toll likely to rise, local sources told AFP .
One official pointed the finger at fighters loyal to the country's former first Vice-President Riek Machar, a longtime rival of President Salva Kiir who has been under house arrest since March 2025.

“The attack on the Bol Bol Boma area in Tonj East County, Warrap State, began late on Saturday,” Machuei Bith, the county's caretaker commissioner, told AFP . He blamed the deaths on fighters from neighbouring Unity State belonging to Machar's SPLA-IO armed group.

"Fifteen civilians and cattle keepers were killed and four armed attackers with SPLA-IO uniforms were also killed," he told AFP . A local police officer confirmed the story on condition of anonymity and said the fighting was still ongoing on Sunday morning. "Further details on casualties from both sides will be shared later on with the media," the officer said.
23 dead in clashes between South Sudan government, opposition forces

Since independence from Sudan in 2011, the world's youngest country has been forced to grapple with various violent conflicts, linked to political infighting, ethnic tensions or competition for resources.
Between 2013 and 2018, the eastern African country was torn apart by a civil war pitting forces loyal to Machar against those supporting Kiir, which left more than 4,00,000 people dead.

articles.title: Giving India’s first practicing woman doctor her due: Kadambini Ganguly​
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Kadambini Ganguly broke barriers to become one of India’s first women physicians to practise Western medicine

As far as trailblazers go, Kadambini Ganguly will figure right on top of several lists. She was a pioneering woman physician, the first to practice successfully in India, a gynaecologist and a social reformer who, equally efficiently, managed a large family as well. The story of Kadambini Ganguly is one of extraordinary achievement, and if told widely, will continue to inspire the young women of today.

In a profile published in Cureus in 2024, the authors point to the influence of the progressive Bramho Samaj movement, initiated by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that helped Kadambini emerge from the shackles of conservative orthodoxy that might have stiffled her immense talent. “This environment, which championed the values of education and gender equality, contributed significantly to shaping her exemplary career and lifelong dedication to social justice,” the article reads. Records of her life acknowledge that she was partly recognised during her lifetime, but also mercilessly criticised and defamed for being a progressive, working woman. The full recognition of her contributions in medicine and the social sector came much later, only in recent decades.

Science, Space & Environment Report: Giving India’s first practicing woman doctor her due: Kadambini Ganguly​. This milestone highlights indigenous research, technological self-reliance, and environmental sustainability.

articles.title: U.S. blocks China’s remote access to AI chips after Nvidia scandal; China slams move
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Nvidia’s provision of chips to companies running data centres in Southeast Asia has come under the spotlight amid questions surrounding founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the CEO of one such Singapore-based company, Megaspeed

The United States has announced new regulations aimed at curbing Chinese firms’ remote access to advanced AI chips through data centres in third party countries, coming amid the scandal surrounding chipmaker Nvidia. Beijing on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) slammed the new restrictions, accusing Washington of “abusing export control measures”.

Nvidia’s provision of chips to companies running data centres in Southeast Asia has come under the spotlight amid questions surrounding founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang , the CEO of one such Singapore-based company, Megaspeed . With Nvidia barred from selling its most advanced chips in China, many Chinese companies instead sought access to its technology through data centres in countries such as Malaysia.

The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced an interim final rule (IFR) “to address remote access” to advanced AI chips and servers, saying it was “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries.”

The new rule was announced days before President Donald Trump’s arrival in Shenzhen for meetings with President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit, which will also see a rare trilateral leaders’ summit along with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The rule states that in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required “to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil”, which it named as “countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.”

China hit out at the moves, calling it “yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry.”

“Such typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction run counter to the common understandings between the two countries, harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, and disrupt global supply chains,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said. “China will do what is necessary to firmly safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.”

China’s Ministry of Commerce in a statement said the new rule would affect the stability of the global semiconductor industry, adding that the U.S. was “misusing export controls to interfere indiscriminately in normal trade cooperation between Chinese enterprises and companies from other countries.” “The U.S. approach runs counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, undermines market rules and the international economic and trade order, and affects the stability of the global semiconductor industry and supply chain,” the statement said.

articles.title: Health Wrap Episode 60 discusses healthcare spending, antimicrobial resistance and more
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The episode discuss trends in healthcare expenditure in India, concerns over the regulation of fertility services, the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance, and the impact of environmental and social conditions on public health

The 60th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu looks at key developments in public including healthcare financing, reproductive health, antimicrobial resistance, tuberculosis, environmental exposures and diabetes care.

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the latest National Health Accounts estimates for 2023–24, which show a substantial increase in government health expenditure and a decline in the share of household out-of-pocket spending nationally. The episode also examines the contrasting trends in Keralam, where household healthcare expenditure has increased and the share of government spending has declined.

The episode looks at the drug regulator’s direction to pharmaceutical companies to comply with revised prices for 137 anti-cancer drugs and the potential implications for treatment costs. It also examines concerns over an illegal human egg collection racket in Telangana, including questions about informed consent, women’s safety and the regulation of assisted reproductive technology centres. Developments in Karnataka’s proposed mid-life women’s health programme and mandatory gynaecological check-ups for girls are also discussed.

Marking World AMR Awareness Week, the episode explores the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance and the need for appropriate antibiotic use, timely diagnosis, infection prevention and surveillance. It also discusses phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to target bacterial infections, and its potential role in addressing infections that do not respond to conventional antibiotics.

The discussion also examines tuberculosis through the lens of social and economic vulnerability, highlighting the importance of nutrition, housing and social support alongside diagnosis and treatment. It looks at the latest figures on domestic funding for India’s TB response, which now accounts for 86% of total spending, even as external funding declines.

The discussion also examines the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women and newborns. A survey of healthcare professionals across five countries found that 98% of Indian clinicians surveyed had treated pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat.

The episode also looks into how fear of diagnosis may discourage people from screening and discusses a Chennai initiative that uses dietary counselling by staff nurses to improve blood sugar control and support long-term diabetes management.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

articles.title: One country, hundreds of dal recipes: exploring India’s diverse lentil traditions
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A look at how the humble ingredient travels through different soils, histories, cultures, climates, and kitchens

From Rajasthan in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east, from Kashmir in the north to Tamil Nadu in the south, India does dal in thousands of ways. There are no fixed proportions to what comes to the table, and everyone’s mother’s recipe is just right. From mamidikaya pappu , or mango dal , to palak dal and dal makhani , there is great diversity in how lentils are prepared across the country. Dal’s resonance here goes beyond the fact that India is the world’s largest producer and consumer of pulses: it is often a reminder of home, a longing for the simple things in life, and a connector of cultures.

That intimacy with dal , however, does not mean everyone makes it the same way — or even that home is where it tastes best. For Harpreet Singh, 26, the dal he cooks at the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) is far better than what is cooked at home. “It’s the ghee that makes the difference,” he says with a laugh, adding that at home, it is rationed. At the temple, five kilos of ghee are added to a quintal of dal . “But the real secret is that we add sarson ka tel [mustard oil] once the dal is boiled, after the mail [froth] on top has been skimmed off,” he says.

Singh’s companion cook adds that it is also the pre-dawn prayers that go into the degchis (wide-mouthed cooking pots) , some of which can hold up to four quintals of dal , which also takes 100 kg of onion, 24 kg of salt, 16 kg of ginger and garlic each, 6 kg of turmeric powder, and 5 kg of khada masala (whole spices). The gurbani (reading of the scriptures) plays on a loudspeaker through the kitchens and service area.

Amritsar’s Golden Temple feeds 70,000 to 80,000 people on weekdays, with the number going to over a lakh on special weekends like amavasya (new moon), and up to 2.5 lakh on a guru’s birthday. In the kitchen, three shifts of about 450 people cook 15-20 quintals of dal daily, over wood-fired stoves. The most popular dal dish here is the mixed variety, which is boiled for six hours. In the langar , a free communal dining hall spread across several rooms and capable of seating 3,000 people at a time, dal is a staple. “Everyone is happy eating it,” says Singh, adding that people also pack food in vessels for patients in hospitals.

From former India cricket captain Harmanpreet Kaur’s fondness for dal and rice while playing for India, to Lok Sabha MP Mahua Moitra bringing her home-cooked dal and bhindi to Parliament, and the slow-cooked, indulgent Dal Raisina served at Rashtrapati Bhavan, dal cuts across social and culinary divides. It is one of India’s most unassuming yet enduring staples — everyday comfort food that can be as humble or elaborate as the occasion demands.

articles.title: Rampur’s Lavi Fair: Storytelling through 300 years of Himalayan trade and tradition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Rampur Bushahr’s Lavi Fair in Himachal Pradesh traces a Himalayan journey from wool and barter to women entrepreneurs and digital payments

What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: Must balance ‘economic patriotism’ with cultural heritage: GJC on PM Modi’s call to stop gold purchases
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) argued that the gold jewellery sector contributes nearly 7-8% to the economy and supports millions of livelihoods

While welcoming Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for prioritising locally-made products and reducing gold imports, the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) has said that India must balance “economic patriotism” and its cultural traditions when it comes to gold jewellery.

It argued that the sector contributes “nearly 7-8%” to the economy and supports “millions of livelihoods”. The GJC was reacting to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent and repeated appeal to all Indians to stop foreign trips and weddings, to buy local, and to only buy gold if necessary.

“The Prime Minister’s appeal for economic patriotism and greater preference for Swadeshi products is timely and welcome,” Rajesh Rokde, Chairman of the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) said.

“While we fully support the Prime Minister’s call for restraint when gold is viewed purely as bullion or an investment instrument, jewellery consumption remains closely linked to culture, craftsmanship, and livelihoods,” Mr. Rokde added.
He said that gold and jewellery hold a unique place in India’s cultural heritage, particularly during festive and wedding seasons, such as the period that India will soon enter in October-December.
“The jewellery industry, contributing nearly 7-8% to the economy and supporting millions of livelihoods, is an integral part of India’s growth story,” Mr. Rokde asserted.
‘People bought less gold, prices fell’: Modi recalls year-old appeal

“As a ₹10 lakh crore industry, the Indian jewellery sector must continue to grow responsibly, with greater transparency, value creation, and alignment with national priorities — balancing economic patriotism with India’s enduring cultural traditions,” he added.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties resume talks to form Israel government
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Likud laid down conditions for a unity government, including no Arab parties and rejection of a Palestinian state, while Gadi Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government

The parties of caretaker Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot launched a new round of talks on Sunday (November 22, 2026) over whether to form a coalition government, with Mr. Netanyahu’s party insisting on keeping his main policies.

Delegations from Mr. Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud began their meeting at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, an AFP journalist on the scene said, following a first round of talks on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

A former Chief of Staff of the army, Mr. Eisenkot has until December 6, 2026, to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after the October 2026 elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Mr. Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow him to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Mr. Eisenkot’s refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Mr. Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign. His ally, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, also reiterated on Saturday (November 21, 2026) his refusal to join a coalition with “Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances”.

On Saturday (November 21, 2026), Yashar presented the resumption of talks as “a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government”, saying Mr. Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options. But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Mr. Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to “all personal attacks and incitement to hatred” targeting the outgoing Prime Minister and his government. It also called for bringing together “all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people”, without the participation of Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to his remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, and a compromise on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

articles.title: Ex-U.K. PM Theresa May tells successor to ‘move on’ from Brexit
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Former British Prime Minister Theresa May said she was “aghast” that Prime Minister Andy Burnham could be considering rejoining the European Union, after he sealed trade and youth mobility deals in Brussels

Ms. May’s remarks came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU’s top officials on Friday (November 20, 2026) sealed deals at a Brussels summit to ease trade and youth mobility. A decade after Britain narrowly voted to leave the bloc, Mr. Burnham has re-energised talk of closer ties ahead of a government 10-year plan for the U.K., set to be unveiled next month.

Ms. May warned that negotiations with the EU risked taking up vast amounts of government time, hampering efforts to tackle other issues. “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU,” she said.

Ms. May, who supported remaining in the 27-member bloc, said government had to respect the result of the 2016 referendum. “When I became prime minister, I was very clear. People have voted for Brexit. We should deliver Brexit,” she told BBC television.

“He (Burnham) wants to pat them (voters) on their head and say ‘you know what? Remember that vote? Well you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come up with the right answer’,” she said. Ms. May was forced to quit in May 2019 after failing to get her Brexit deal through parliament.

“My message to him (Burnham) really is: People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” she added. Mr. Burnham, who has been in office since July 2026, has committed to his predecessor Keir Starmer’s “red lines” on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement. But pro-Brexit campaigners fear he will push at some point to rejoin the 27-nation grouping.
Europe Minister Hamish Falconer said the world had changed since 2016, and the U.K. needed to “think over the long term about our relationship with Europe”.

“That’s why the prime minister is going to set out more next month as part of the 10-year plan about the long-term relationship between the UK and the EU,” he told Sky News . But he insisted the British people “are going to be the boss of every stage of this”.
“We are talking, as the prime minister was clear, about the long term. We will have a general election before then. People will be able to express their views,” he said.
Following Mr. Burnham’s EU deals, legislation to allow the U.K. to align with certain EU rules, including on food standards, is due to be introduced in parliament this week.

articles.title: Nvidia faces U.S. accounting probe amid deepening turmoil: media
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Securities and Exchange Commission inquiry is in its early stages, U.S. media reported, after Jensen Huang’s resignation as chief executive and a 14% fall in Nvidia shares on Friday (November 20, 2026)

U.S. securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to U.S. media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported on Saturday (November 21, 2026), citing people briefed on the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.

Questions about Nvidia’s financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers’ billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, U.S. media reported.

The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company’s significant business there. It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of working for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully.
Nvidia’s board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive, and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Huang’s departure.

The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world’s most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom. Nvidia shares plunged 14% on Friday (November 20, 2026), bringing their losses for the week to more than 20%.

U.S. President Donald Trump nevertheless called on Friday (November 20, 2026) for Mr. Huang to be reinstated. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Mr. Trump told reporters. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation.

articles.title: COP 31 talks fail as EU, others reject any climate deal without language on a fossil fuel phase-out
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: EU, Panama among about 130 parties that refuse to accept COP President’s consensus cover text, alleges that it “greenwashes” fossil fuels; India, China, Saudi Arabia are on the other side of the divide

A standoff on a fossil fuel phase-out prevented countries at COP 31, the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkiye, from achieving any consensus agreement on future climate action on Sunday (November 22, 2026), despite the conference running a record 48 hours into overtime.

The European Union led objections to COP 31 President Murat Kurum’s consensus cover text that failed to include any explicit language about moving away from fossil fuels. The EU’s stance was reportedly supported by about 130 countries.

On the other side of the divide, India is among the nations that supported the proposed cover text, as they want to keep using fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, with Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav stressing that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation.”

“We express profound disappointment with the final draft COP31 cover decision or Antalya Pact. At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short,” Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said, speaking on behalf of the EU.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach… We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” he added.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome, it needs the consensus of all parties.

Panama also formally objected to the text, saying that as a country battling droughts and other perilous impacts of climate change, the lack of any commitment to keep the rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees C with firm action on phasing out fossil fuels was “a setback”.

“Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it weighs too much upon technologies such as CCUS [carbon capture utilisation and storage] instead of calling for deep changes, and three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback,” said Ana Aguilar, Panama’s chief climate negotiator.

On the other side, Saudi Arabia, China, and India are among the countries that are against explicit language on fossil fuel and expressed comfort with the way the cover text language was framed, while also expressing misgivings about the lack of clarity on adaptation finance. The countries are part of the Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) coalition, who are insistent on the use of fossil fuel in the foreseeable future to further their economies, but have also significantly deployed renewable energy.

Indian Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said that India’s voice had shaped the draft COP 31 outcome, especially on food security, livelihoods, and cultural practices recognised in action on methane. However, in a post on X, he emphasised that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation. Energy transitions must be nationally determined, just and equitable, backed by finance, technology and capacity-building for developing countries.”

articles.title: Thumba to Kourou, over 60 years of space partnership
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: India and France are charting a shared space future

For over 60 years, France and India have shared one of the longest-standing and most trusted space partnerships in the world. At a time when the international environment has become increasingly complex, this partnership matters more than ever before.

Since 1998, their strategic partnership has reposed on defence cooperation — from the Alouette III/Chetak and Rafale aircraft to Scorpène submarines built in India — and people-to-people ties, expanding over time to include artificial intelligence, the blue economy, and much more. What is remarkable about their special global strategic partnership is that, at the core of their national security doctrine, they both share the concept of strategic autonomy. Strategic autonomy does not mean isolating oneself from partners. On the contrary, it means building up one’s own capacities, own analysis, and own decision-making process to be a useful and reliable partner. France has consistently backed India’s rise as a global power, including its permanent seat at the UN Security Council.

articles.title: Why a shortage of clinical psychologists in Keralam govt hospitals is leaving people with intellectual disabilities waiting for certificates
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: As per the last Kerala Disability Census in 2015, there are about 80,000 persons with various intellectual challenges. However, government hospitals and medical college hospitals in the State currently have only 22 clinical psychologists to conduct IQ assessment tests

People with intellectual disabilities in Keralam are struggling to obtain and renew disability certificates due to a severe shortage of clinical psychologists in government hospitals to conduct Intelligence Quotient (IQ) assessment tests.

As per the latest disability assessment guidelines issued by the Union government’s Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, differently-abled children must undergo assessment tests at least thrice before they turn 18 to obtain permanent disability certificates. During all these assessment phases, an IQ test is a must. However, there are only 22 clinical psychologists under the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) and the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) put together – 17 under the DHS and the rest under the DME.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Even a low base effect could not push India’s oil and gas sectors into growth

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Editorial Context: Core accountability: On core sector performance. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

1. Core Context & Background: Climate action has to be timely, with adequate resources and monitoring

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Editorial Context: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.
